    Summary and Schedule

    Good data organisation is the foundation of any research or administrative project. Most of us keep data in spreadsheets, laid out the way people like to read them. Computers need data laid out differently. So do AI tools, which read data as literally as any program, and then report their answers with confidence.

    This lesson teaches how to organise data so that people, programs and AI tools all read it the way you intend. It uses one synthetic dataset throughout: Enterococci counts at four Durban beaches, recorded by two field assistants in two very different, very messy spreadsheets.

    In this lesson you will learn to:

    • lay out data tables that computers can use;
    • recognise and fix the common spreadsheet mistakes;
    • record dates unambiguously;
    • prevent and find errors with data validation, sorting and filtering;
    • export data to open formats;
    • write a data dictionary, and use it as context for AI tools;
    • organise project folders, name files and protect raw data;
    • decide what data may be given to an AI tool, and keep AI-assisted work reproducible.

    You will not learn statistics, plotting or programming in this lesson.

    Prerequisite

    Prerequisites

    A computer with a spreadsheet program (Excel, LibreOffice Calc or Google Sheets). No programming experience is needed. Download the data before you start; see Setup.

    Prerequisite

    Data

    Download this data file to your computer: https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/2252083

    About the data

    The data for this lesson is a part of the Data Carpentry Ecology workshop. It is a teaching version of the Portal Database. The data in this lesson is a subset of the teaching version that has been intentionally ‘messed up’ for this lesson.

    The data for this lesson and the workshop are in the Portal Project Teaching Database available on FigShare, with a CC-BY license available for reuse.

    Ernest, M., Brown, J., Valone, T., and White, E.P. (2017). Portal Project Teaching Database. Version 6. Figshare. DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.1314459.v6

    Prerequisite

    Software

    To interact with spreadsheets, we can use LibreOffice, Microsoft Excel, Gnumeric, OpenOffice.org, or other programs. Commands may differ a bit between programs, but the general ideas for thinking about spreadsheets are the same.

    For this lesson, if you don’t have a spreadsheet program already, you can use LibreOffice. It’s a free, open source spreadsheet program.

    Windows

    • Download the Installer
      • Install LibreOffice by going to the installation page. The version for Windows should automatically be selected. Click Download Version X.X.X (whichever is the most recent version). You will go to a page that asks about a donation, but you don’t need to make one. Your download should begin automatically.
    • Install LibreOffice
    • Once the installer is downloaded, double click on it and LibreOffice should install.
